title: Unless I wash you: cleansing and share with Christ
english: We have set forth the proposition that when a soul of this kind happens to be encountered, it is necessary to recognize the natural good things belonging to it as a cosmos in its own right, through which it was healed by the divine, stored up in its inaccessible parts for everything except the word of the high priest, and called its desires. Moreover, upon all these things, the enemy who has gained mastery in the ancient contest, having afflicted the soul that wages war not well for itself but rather has been left behind worthily by divine aid, extends himself through the power of his activity into evil things, drags away the ruling faculty and leaves the soul that has departed from God desolate of good things. And the nations, according to the place, are to be understood allegorically as the crowd of vices that have entered into the formed ruling faculty, so as to be a receptacle and true sanctification of God for the pure mind wishing to rest again. These nations God utterly forbids from entering the church; for what else could we consider more forbidden by God from entering into a soul numbered in the church of God than the works and the mind of the flesh, which are truly nations hostile to God? For "the flesh wars against the spirit," "the mind of the flesh is enmity toward God"; "for to the law of God it is not subject, nor indeed can it be." They groaned because of famine and because of little food, the soul turning back and leaving behind provided the most precious things. But how did the previously mentioned desires, taken away by the enemies, provide for the purchase of food? Yet "the enemy stretched forth his hand against all things," and having been satisfied with taking what he wished, he left the rest behind, in exchange for which they bought food.

Jerusalem prays, Lord, look upon my shame, since you have destroyed the world by famine. Perhaps different desires preceded, first the foretold things which the enemy had stretched out his hand upon, secondly each person's own desires from among the people; and the common things were taken, but instead of the particular things, each one bought food for himself. Moreover, for guidance, just as Esau sold his birthright for red stew, of which he became surnamed (Edom meaning Red Earth; and indeed he became earthly, having despised the birthrights, having made earthly things which Jacob, as necessary, transferred to him in a second discourse because he happened to be in a body), so also Jerusalem. But the one who gives Jacob the worthy to obtain, which things he had desired, even if he did not previously choose them; but the people of Jerusalem have given indeed also themselves because of food, but not having sanctified this construction, but the Babylonians who were about to insult the given desires. For Jacob knows how to adorn the things from Esau, but the Babylonians do not use the given things for their own good. And so the soul, through lack of necessities, rejects the divine teachings to those who, out of curiosity, desire to learn for slander and mockery. 30 He has shown the one upon the conflagration of the strongest buildings touching or the fall of the superior ones in it of the city, to the soul and to those outside as if burning with the calamities. He also indicates the conception of those who have been subdued into slavery like in a field with nets,

Those who did not make good use of freedom. For these, "not stretching forward to the things that are ahead, but forgetting the things that are behind," they turned away from glory into dishonor, from freedom into slavery, and have become instead of honorable ones, darkened and obscure through dishonor and insolence; because of these things the city has fallen into endless grief. 31 Providence, he says, has not slept over my impious deeds; for God, as if taking them into his hands, has intertwined them through examination with the works of recompense. And these things have become to me like a yoke placed upon the neck and slavery imposed upon it; for just as I served slavery to Nebuchadnezzar, my sins are slavery, therefore I have become weak, delivered over to these things whose dominion I cannot withstand. And shortly after: His yoke upon my neck is shown. But it is indicated through the present expression that the things spoken of as concerning our passions ought to be taken more tropically in regard to God. For how otherwise could the impieties of Jerusalem be understood, joined to the hand of God, except tropically? For no one could speak these things literally. And how is it not absurd, that while the city of Jerusalem is said to lift up its neck tropically, the things spoken as concerning God do not hear the same manner? title: Defilement, washings, and the path back to holiness
english:
The sins that have weakened me, having cast me away from the divine oversight and delivered me into the service of the sovereign of evils, are such that, due to the boundless and infinite nature of wickedness, I cannot fully minister to her nor satisfy her with sufficient provision. Indeed, sin truly humbles and presses down upon one, causing the gaze to fall low; yet the yoke and the ever-present, piercing conscience continually sting and urge one not to relent, stripping away all boldness. Moreover, as he says, permission and the strength with which I did not act well have been granted, and I behold the evils that hold me dissolving.  
He did not take them from my midst (for even if I had been deprived of them, I could have used them elsewhere), but in my midst he judged them guilty for the very acts of impiety I committed. My chosen ones have endured the most severe trials, having drunk the wine of the Lord’s wrath, which He trod in the winepress until it filled me and the virgin daughter of the most royal Judah. One might say that the strong are those who wage war and defend the fatherland, while the elect are the noble or the wise. He clarifies the winepress by referencing what was said in the Psalms concerning the punishment of sinners: “A cup in the hand of the Lord, full of unmixed wine, mingled with spice,” pouring from the one being punished upon the one being punished, until all the sinners of the earth drink, while the remnants of the vintage remain for the lesser sinners still existing, to whom finally “the one who treads the winepress” shall be emptied.  
It is not difficult to see how the Lord trod the winepress upon the virgin daughter of Judah.

For indeed, as the proverb says, “Each one reaps what he sows,” and so too, perhaps, each one harvests what he cultivates. The one who produces superior wine will rejoice in the fruits of his own labor. But the one who cultivates “the vineyard of Sodom and the vine-dressing of Gomorrah, bearing fruit for the tribe of bitterness, yielding a cluster of gall and a wrath that shields cannot withstand—all of which the Lord gathers together”—into a single winepress, where his evil deeds are trodden underfoot and crushed, such a person, in keeping with such fruits, drinks in order to vomit up the gall, the bitterness, and the wrath. And he drinks, according to Jeremiah, to purge himself; according to Isaiah, to awaken and clothe himself in kindred glory. For the Lord does not tread the winepress in vain, and especially not for the virgin daughter of Judah. 34 Thus, the soul, having received many gifts from its Creator—both natural and chosen—yet deprived of them through wickedness and suffering punishment, acknowledges what it has endured. And the one called to be broken in the time of retribution is the moment when, according to Ezekiel, “none of the righteous deeds which the righteous one has done shall be remembered in the day of his sin.” Mourning what has befallen her, she is benefited, for to those who mourn and weep belongs the promise of consolation and laughter. 35 She declared that the cause of her lamentations was the absence of the one who turns back her soul—namely, the one who restores it according to Symmachus. And she says that her sons have perished through the strengthening of the enemy, by means of which they were exiled; for although we are pious, we do not prevail, for the weak, as they progress, are destroyed and utterly broken beneath the feet—“becoming thin as dust before the face of the wind,”

And as clay in the streets, becoming thin. For in proportion as we sin, it is nourished and gains strength; but when transgressions cease, it is, as it were, destroyed by famine. And from the opposing forces, the divine powers, when we act well, we strengthen ourselves and pursue those who sin. Therefore Symmachus, instead of "the obliterated ones," delivered "deserts." One might say these things of a contemplative soul that has attained the word of true divinity and, through slackness, has lost this joyful word and all its fruits, which it names as its children, because it has been strengthened against the evil that opposes it. Zion says the mountain, and the people of Jacob, and the mother-city Jerusalem. And God commanded Jacob with commandments by which, when transgressed, he was encircled by enemies; and according to Symmachus and another edition of the Seventy, the Lord commanded that those who oppress him should be round about him, namely, the powers appointed to do evil. The uncleanness of Jerusalem through sin, as through a sewer, he has shown. And in the midst, he speaks either of Zion and Jacob, or of the whole mountain as middle (for in part it is built upon), and of the whole people; now this signifies Jacob, the twelve scepters. And according to the word, it is possible to take Zion and Jerusalem in two ways: either the places or the inhabitants. But if Zion is a place, her hands are her works, for example.

title: Purity restored and the soul share with the Word
english: Agriculture and any handiwork, he says, are left spread out and not gathered together, failing to perform the proper work with their hands, as if in an idle and desolate land. If, however, he is speaking of those dwelling within, the hands would be farmers and laborers, not withdrawing their hands from work due to surrounding circumstances. But if the hands of Zion are being counted, how much more the members according to Scripture of God are to be regarded. And indeed, the mountain itself, as it were, groans with the people, lacking comfort from God or from a holy man. The mouth of the Lord must be heeded in the prophets, of whom Isaiah, who exists, declared: "For the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things." Yet Jerusalem, rewarded by the Savior as "having slain the prophets," moreover, provoked the mouth of the Lord to bitter pains by delivering them over. But the God who "seeks the blood of the prophets" delivers her to afflictions from wars and again to captivities, handing over her young men and virgins. Therefore, for what she has suffered, she confesses before others, presenting herself as an example to these, so that those who have learned God’s righteousness may not suffer similar things. After the perceptible, interpret virgins as those living in incorruptibility, and young men as those prospering in virtue. For often the holy ones also suffer with those responsible. The lovers, namely those who are such, Ezekiel has declared to Jerusalem, whom he calls Olivet, saying: "Thus says the Lord Lord: Behold, I will stir up your lovers against you from every side, sons of Babylon and all the Chaldeans." For these, though formerly friends by divine providence, have turned into enemies.

It often happens, under the impulse of love, that one turns into hatred; for he speaks concerning Samaria thus: “And Oholah played the harlot away from me, and she set herself upon her lovers, the Assyrians”; and shortly after: “Therefore he delivered her into the hands of her lovers, into the hands of the sons of Assyria.” He also speaks concerning Jerusalem: “And her sister Oholibah saw it, and she defiled her illicit affection more than the harlotry of her sister, and she set herself upon the sons of the Assyrians.” 41 In the prophecy, indeed, the soul grieves as if being persuaded of obvious things; but in the present Lamentation, as though these things have already come to pass, she grieves bitterly and, through sin, confesses that she has brought upon herself the utmost bitterness of God’s goodness, as if she, who was abundantly fruitful, had been made barren, and as if the most terrible thing—war by hostile hand—had befallen her. Since personification is employed, one should not seek a literal city whose womb bore children and whose heart was loosened. 42 He divides the word into eight parts, addressing Jerusalem toward her enemies, whom he wishes to hear, and toward God. But what does he urge upon the enemies for their hearing? And what does he say to God about them, as if they had rejoiced? Perhaps, therefore (since “her transgression and Israel’s transgression have become the instruction of the nations to provoke them to jealousy,” and “when the fullness of the nations has entered in, then all Israel will be saved”), he speaks prophetically first to those from the nations, and then to God concerning the second matters: “You were left behind to suffer so that you might take possession of the land, and I have become, through you, an enemy of God, though according to the election, beloved for the sake of the fathers, I continue to exist.”

Therefore, you have heard my lamentation and perceived its cause; for I am entirely consumed on account of your salvation, left bereft, lacking the one who continually comforts me amid the trials of evil. Now the "leader has departed from Judah, and he who was reckoned from his loins" has come—He to whom belonged "the things stored up," "the expectation of the nations"—at whose blood’s vengeance, no one remains to console Jerusalem. This means: let not their wickedness be allowed to persist unchecked; rather, may it be granted to you in oversight, as if one were to pray for wounds to come before a physician, in order to attain complete healing. For this is the whole: blessed above all is the one who does not sin, and second, blessed is the one whom God examines wholly for wickedness. Moreover, glean after the vintage the small remnants of the grape clusters left behind, as the poor do. Just as when you carefully inspected my vines, you cleansed them, removing every worthless shoot down to the tiniest bits—“the cluster of gall and the bunch of bitterness”—so too, let me glean after my enemies. This would be beneficial to me, for if they were fully saved alongside me, then I, according to your judgment, O Lord, would obtain salvation’s verdict; whom I see, I am deeply grieved and condemn myself, the oversight I need from you. Likewise, as David said: “He will utterly crush all the horns of the sinners.” Now he speaks of the rulers, in whom resides the strength of the nation…
